scenes.say: One man had hiccups for sixty-eight years.
A hiccup is your diaphragm, the muscle under your lungs, suddenly yanking down.
scenes.heading: WHAT HAPPENS

scenes.say: A split second later, your vocal cords snap shut. That's the hic.
scenes.heading: THEN

scenes.say: But why do we have this reflex at all? One theory goes back to tadpoles.
scenes.heading: BUT WHY?

scenes.say: Tadpoles breathe water through gills by closing their throat in almost the same move. We may have inherited the switch.
scenes.heading: THE THEORY

scenes.say: Another theory: babies hiccup a lot, and it may help push extra air out of the stomach while drinking milk.
scenes.heading: THEORY 2

scenes.say: As for that man, Charles Osborne, he hiccuped from 1922 to 1990. An estimated four hundred thirty million hiccups.
scenes.label: hiccups, 1922 to 1990
